title: Why food spoils and how to keep it safe

say: Why food spoils, and how to keep it safe.
This is the video for module 1 of Food Preservation and Storage.
Food does not go bad by magic. Every spoiled tomato has a cause you can name.
First, microbes: tiny living bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Some can make people ill without changing how the food looks.

panel.heading: Five causes of spoilage
items: Microbes: bacteria, yeasts and moulds
Enzymes: cut yam browns, banana goes black
Air: oils and groundnuts turn rancid
Pests: weevils, cockroaches, rats
Damage: bruises and cracks let germs in

say: Second, enzymes, natural substances inside food. They make a cut yam turn brown and a banana go soft and black.

say: Microbes need food, water, warmth, time and, for most of them, air. Take one away and they slow down or stop. Every method in this course does that.

panel.heading: Take away what microbes need
items: Microbes need food, water, warmth, time, air
Drying and salting take away water
Fridge and freezer take away warmth
Vinegar and fermenting make food sour
Danger zone: 5°C to 60°C

say: The WHO Five Keys poster marks 5 to 60 degrees Celsius as the danger zone, where bacteria multiply quickly. A Nigerian kitchen afternoon sits inside it. So rice left on the stove overnight can be unsafe even when it smells fine.

say: There is no single best method. Choose by the food, how long it must keep, your power, and whether you will sell it. For days or a few weeks, the fridge, light salting or fridge pickles may be enough.

For months, you need freezing, proper drying, hard smoking or real jam. Several small hurdles together are often safer than one. And remember, no method makes bad food good again. Start fresh every time.
Check these five keys before any preserving job. Keep hands, surfaces and tools clean. Keep raw meat and fish apart from cooked food. Boil soups and stews.
Never leave cooked food out for more than 2 hours, and never thaw frozen food at room temperature. Use safe water and fresh food.

panel.heading: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
items: Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials

say: Botulism is a rare but very serious illness. WHO explains that the bacterium grows only where there is no air. A sealed jar or a layer of oil shuts air out.

panel.heading: The hidden danger in jars and oil
items: The bacterium grows only without air
It cannot grow below pH 4.6 (acidic food)
Low-acid: garlic, ginger, onion, pepper, fish
Oil on top does not preserve food
Weakness, blurred vision: hospital at once

say: It will not grow in acidic food, below pH 4.6.

say: So the risk is low-acid food, such as garlic, ginger, onions, pepper paste without vinegar, fish and meat, sealed up at room temperature. It may look and smell normal.

say: Tiredness, weakness, blurred vision or trouble swallowing after eating preserved food means hospital at once. And never give honey to a baby under 1 year old.

say: A bulging lid means gas from microbes. Mould roots go deeper than you can see, so do not scrape it off and eat.

panel.heading: Signs that mean: throw it away
items: Bulging lid, or liquid spurts out
Mould on jam, pickles, ogi or dried food
Cloudiness, bubbles or slime in a clear pickle
Off or rotten smell
Mouldy or discoloured groundnuts or maize

say: Slime or unexpected cloudiness, or an off smell, means spoilage. Never taste to check.

panel.heading: Signs that mean: throw it away

say: Mouldy groundnuts or maize may carry aflatoxin, a mould poison. Wrap anything suspicious in a bag, put it in a covered bin, and wash your hands.

say: To remember. Name the cause, then take away what microbes need. Sort out damaged items early. Food that looks and smells fine can still be unsafe. And if you are ever unsure, keep it cold, use it quickly, or throw it out.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Five causes: microbes, enzymes, air, pests, damage
Every method takes away a microbe need
Remove damaged items early
Food that smells fine can still be unsafe
No low-acid food sealed or under oil in the heat

say: Now practise. Walk through your kitchen and name the cause of spoilage in three foods. Map five foods your household wastes to a method. Then check every home-made jar for danger signs, and post the Five Keys near your preparation area.
